summary.en: The Sun enters Makara: the harvest festival that marks the start of Uttarayana, the Sun's northward journey.

traditions.en: Families wake early for a bath, many in a river, and offer water to the Sun. Sesame and jaggery sweets (til-gud, gajak, rewari) are made and shared, and khichdi is cooked and given away. Kites fill the sky in Gujarat and Rajasthan, where the day is Uttarayan. In Punjab the evening before is Lohri; in Tamil Nadu the same day is Thai Pongal and in Assam it is Magh Bihu. Giving warm clothes, blankets and grain to those who need them is a common part of the day.

story.en: The story told for this day is of the Sun god, Surya, visiting his son Shani. The two had long been distant, and Surya's journey into Makara, the sign Shani rules, is remembered as a father setting aside old differences to see his son. Shani is said to have welcomed him with black sesame, the only thing he had, and Surya accepted it gladly. That is why sesame is at the heart of the day's food and gifts. The day is also remembered in the Mahabharata: Bhishma, who could choose the moment of his passing, waited on his bed of arrows for Uttarayana to begin. And many tell that on this day the Ganga, following King Bhagiratha, reached the sea at Ganga Sagar, where a great bathing fair is held every year.

en: The day before, make til-gud laddoos or buy gajak and rewari, and soak rice and moong dal for khichdi.
Wake before sunrise and bathe; add a few sesame seeds to the bath water if your family does.
Offer water to the rising Sun from a copper vessel, facing east.
Cook khichdi and share it, along with sesame sweets, with neighbours and anyone who visits.
Set aside grain, sesame, a blanket or warm clothes to give to someone who needs them.
Spend the afternoon outdoors: fly kites in Gujarat and Rajasthan, or visit family elsewhere.
Greet elders with til-gud; in Maharashtra the words are 'til-gul ghya, god god bola' (take sweets and speak sweetly).

greeting.en: May the Sun's new journey bring warmth to your home. Happy Makar Sankranti!

summary.en: Magha Shukla Chaturthi: Ganesh Jayanti, the birth of Ganesha, kept as Maghi Ganeshotsav in Maharashtra and Konkan.
summary.mr: माघ शुक्ल चतुर्थी: गणेश जयंती, गणपतीचा जन्मदिवस; महाराष्ट्र आणि कोकणात माघी गणेशोत्सव.

traditions.en: Ganesha temples, the Ashtavinayaka shrines and Siddhivinayak among them, hold a festival with abhishekam and processions, and many homes and mandals bring an image for one or a few days. Sesame and jaggery modaks and laddoos are offered, so the day is also called Tilkund Chaturthi.
traditions.mr: अष्टविनायक, सिद्धिविनायक यांसह गणपती मंदिरांत अभिषेक आणि पालख्या होतात, आणि अनेक घरे व मंडळे एक किंवा काही दिवसांसाठी गणपती आणतात. तिळगुळाचे मोदक आणि लाडू नैवेद्य म्हणून दाखवले जातात, म्हणून या दिवसाला तिलकुंद चतुर्थी असेही म्हणतात.

summary.en: The seventh day of bright Magha: the Sun's birthday, when Surya turns his chariot north.

traditions.en: People bathe at dawn, traditionally placing seven leaves of the arka (erukku) plant on the head and shoulders while bathing. A chariot with seven horses is drawn in kolam or rangoli at the doorstep, and the Sun is worshipped as the rising light, with a lamp and a sweet pongal or kheer cooked in the open sunlight in some homes. Temples hold a Surya procession: at Tirumala the deity is taken out on seven vahanas through the day, from dawn to night, for the 'one-day Brahmotsavam'. The day is also called Surya Jayanti and Achala Saptami.

story.en: The story told for Ratha Saptami is that on this day Surya was born to the sage Kashyapa and Aditi, and so is called Aditya. His chariot is drawn by seven horses, said to stand for the seven days of the week, or for the seven colours of light, and it has a single wheel, the year turning. From Ratha Saptami, tradition says, the Sun turns his chariot fully northward, and the days grow warmer toward spring. A second story tells of King Yashovarma of Kamboja, whose only son was unwell for a long time; on a sage's advice the prince kept the Ratha Saptami observance, and is remembered as having grown strong. The arka leaves of the bath are a reminder of Bhishma, who is said to have received them in his last days.

en: The evening before, draw a seven-horse chariot rangoli or kolam at the entrance.
Wake before dawn and bathe; if your family does, place seven arka leaves, with a little rice and sesame, on your head and shoulders while bathing.
Face the rising Sun and offer water from a copper vessel, reciting the Aditya Hridayam or simply the twelve names of Surya.
Light a lamp and offer a sweet pongal or kheer, cooked in sunlight if you can.
Share the prasad and spend some time outdoors in the morning sun.

greeting.en: May the rising Sun light your path. Happy Ratha Saptami!

summary.en: The great night of Shiva, kept with fasting, night-long worship and the chanting of 'Om Namah Shivaya'.

traditions.en: Devotees fast through the day, some taking only fruit and milk, and stay awake through the night. Temples hold four worships (prahara puja) across the night, bathing the Shiva linga in milk, curd, honey, ghee and water and offering bilva leaves. At home, families chant 'Om Namah Shivaya', read or listen to Shiva stories and sing bhajans. In Tamil Nadu temples hold the night's four abhishekams; in Kerala, the Aluva riverbank fills with people keeping vigil; in the North, kanwariyas carry Ganga water to Shiva temples. The fast is broken the next morning.

story.en: Several stories are told for this night. In one, when the gods and asuras churned the ocean for nectar, a deadly poison, Halahala, rose first and threatened every living thing. Shiva drank it to protect the world, and Parvati held his throat so it would not go further; his throat turned blue, and he is called Neelakantha. The gods kept awake all night to watch over him, and devotees keep that vigil still. Another story tells of a hunter lost in the forest at night who climbed a bilva tree to stay safe. Restless, he plucked leaves and dropped them, not knowing a Shiva linga stood below; by morning he had kept a night's worship without meaning to, and his heart was changed. Many also remember this as the night of Shiva and Parvati's wedding.

en: Decide how you will fast: a full fast, fruit and milk, or one simple meal; elders, children and anyone unwell often keep a light version.
Gather bilva leaves, milk, water, curd, honey, flowers and a lamp.
In the evening, bathe and visit a Shiva temple, or set up a small linga or picture at home.
Bathe the linga with water and milk, offer bilva leaves and flowers, and light the lamp.
Chant 'Om Namah Shivaya', read the Shiva Purana or listen to bhajans; many keep awake through the four quarters of the night.
The night's main worship is at Nishita, around midnight; the app's day view shows the time.
Break the fast the next morning after a bath and a short prayer, with simple food.

greeting.en: Om Namah Shivaya. Peaceful wishes on Maha Shivaratri.

summary.en: The bonfire on the night of Phalguna Purnima, remembering Prahlad, on the eve of Holi.

traditions.en: Neighbourhoods build a pyre of wood and dung cakes in a common square in the days before. On the evening of the full moon, after Bhadra has passed, women tie raw cotton thread around it and walk around it, offering water, coconut, grain, roli and new wheat or gram. The fire is lit at the chosen time and people roast green wheat and chana in it to share. Many carry home a little of the fire or ash. It is a night for gathering with neighbours before the colours of the next day.

story.en: The story told for this night is of Prahlad, a young prince devoted to Vishnu. His father, the asura king Hiranyakashipu, had won a boon that made him almost impossible to defeat, and he demanded to be worshipped in Vishnu's place. Prahlad would not stop praying to Vishnu, and his father's attempts to turn him all failed. At last Hiranyakashipu's sister, Holika, who had a shawl that the fire could not burn, sat in a blazing pyre with Prahlad on her lap. The story goes that the shawl flew from her to cover Prahlad; he came out unharmed and Holika did not. The bonfire remembers the boy's steady faith, and the story continues a little later with Vishnu appearing as Narasimha.

en: Join your neighbourhood's Holika, or build a small one safely with your community; keep water nearby.
Prepare a thali with water, roli, rice, flowers, raw cotton thread, a coconut, jaggery and new wheat ears or green chana.
Check the Holika Dahan time in the day view: it is lit after sunset on the full moon, after Bhadra ends.
Before it is lit, wind the cotton thread around the pyre while walking around it three or seven times.
Offer the water and the thali items, and fold your hands in a short prayer.
Once it is lit, roast wheat ears and chana in the fire and share them.
Keep children back from the fire, and make sure it is put out safely at the end.

greeting.en: On Holika Dahan, wishing you the steady faith of Prahlad.

summary.en: The festival of colours, the morning after Holika Dahan: spring, play and setting differences aside.

traditions.en: Friends, families and whole streets play with coloured powder (gulal) and coloured water, chasing one another with pichkaris and water balloons. The greeting is 'Holi hai!' and 'Bura na mano, Holi hai' (don't mind, it's Holi). Homes make gujiya, malpua, dahi bhalle and thandai. By afternoon everyone washes up, dresses in fresh clothes and visits relatives and friends. In Braj, around Mathura and Vrindavan, Holi is celebrated for days, with Lathmar Holi at Barsana and flower Holi in the temples.

story.en: Holi carries two stories. The first follows from the night before: the morning after Holika's fire, people celebrated Prahlad's safe return, and the colours are that celebration. The second is the story of Krishna in Braj. As a child Krishna worried that his dark skin set him apart from fair Radha. His mother Yashoda laughed and told him to colour Radha's face with whatever colour he liked. He did, and Radha and the gopis coloured him back, and the game spread through Gokul and Vrindavan. That playful spirit, in which no one minds being coloured and everyone is equal for a day, is what Holi is about. Coming at the end of winter, it is also a celebration of spring.

en: A day or two before, buy natural or skin-safe gulal, and make or order gujiya and thandai.
Before playing, rub coconut or mustard oil on your skin and hair so colours wash off easily; wear old clothes.
In the morning, start with a small prayer and a pinch of gulal offered to Krishna or the family deity.
Greet elders by touching their feet and putting a little gulal on their cheeks or feet.
Play with friends and neighbours; ask before colouring someone, and keep colour away from eyes and away from animals.
Around midday, wash, change into clean clothes and share sweets.
In the afternoon or evening, visit relatives and friends, and make peace with anyone you have drifted from.

greeting.en: Wishing you a Holi full of colour, laughter and old friends. Happy Holi!

summary.en: Phalguna Krishna Panchami, five days after Holi: Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh play with colours.
summary.mr: फाल्गुन कृष्ण पंचमी, होळीनंतर पाचवा दिवस: महाराष्ट्र आणि मध्य प्रदेशात रंगांचा उत्सव.

traditions.en: Where Holi itself is the bonfire night and Dhulivandan the day after, the play with colours in Maharashtra comes on Ranga Panchami: gulal and coloured water, music, and in Indore and other cities long processions (gair) spraying colour over the crowds.
traditions.mr: होळी म्हणजे होलिकादहनाची रात्र आणि धुलिवंदन दुसरा दिवस; महाराष्ट्रात रंग खेळणे रंगपंचमीला होते: गुलाल, रंगीत पाणी, संगीत, आणि इंदूरसारख्या शहरांत गर्दीवर रंग उडवत निघणाऱ्या गेरी मिरवणुका.

summary.en: Chaitra Shukla Pratipada: the Marathi New Year, welcomed with a gudi raised at every home.
summary.mr: चैत्र शुक्ल प्रतिपदा: मराठी नववर्ष, प्रत्येक घरी गुढी उभारून स्वागत.

traditions.en: At sunrise families raise the gudi: a bamboo staff dressed with a bright silk cloth, neem leaves, a garland of sugar crystals (gathi) and marigolds, topped with an upturned copper or silver pot, and set up at a window or door. The day begins with an oil bath and a bite of neem leaves mixed with jaggery. Rangoli is drawn, puran poli or shrikhand-puri is cooked, and in cities people join Shobha Yatras in nine-yard sarees and pheta turbans. It is one of the three and a half most favoured days (sade teen muhurta) of the year for new beginnings.
traditions.mr: सूर्योदयाला कुटुंबे गुढी उभारतात: बांबूच्या काठीला रेशमी वस्त्र, कडुलिंबाची पाने, साखरेची गाठी आणि झेंडूची माळ बांधून वर तांब्याचा किंवा चांदीचा कलश उपडा ठेवला जातो आणि ती खिडकीत किंवा दारात उभी केली जाते. दिवसाची सुरुवात अभ्यंगस्नानाने आणि गूळ घालून कडुलिंबाची पाने खाऊन होते. रांगोळी काढली जाते, पुरणपोळी किंवा श्रीखंड-पुरी केली जाते आणि शहरांत नऊवारी साड्या व फेटे घालून लोक शोभायात्रांमध्ये सामील होतात. वर्षातील साडेतीन मुहूर्तांपैकी हा एक मुहूर्त आहे.

en: Take an oil bath at dawn.
Raise the gudi at the door or window, facing out.
Offer haldi-kunku and flowers, and eat neem leaves with jaggery.
Take the gudi down before sunset.
mr: हळद-कुंकू, फुले वाहा आणि गुळासह कडुलिंबाची पाने खा.

summary.en: Chaitra Gauri: for a month from Chaitra Shukla Tritiya, Gauri is welcomed into Maharashtrian homes.
summary.mr: चैत्रगौर: चैत्र शुक्ल तृतीयेपासून महिनाभर गौरी माहेरी येते असे मानून तिचे स्वागत.

traditions.en: Gauri is said to visit her parents' home for the month of Chaitra. An image of her is seated on a decorated swing (jhula) and, on a convenient day of the month, women hold a haldi-kunku: friends are invited, given haldi and kumkum, soaked gram (bhijavlele harbhare), raw-mango panha and kairichi dal, and a small gift.
traditions.mr: चैत्र महिन्यात गौरी माहेरी येते असे मानले जाते. तिची मूर्ती सजवलेल्या झोपाळ्यावर बसवली जाते आणि महिन्यातील सोयीच्या दिवशी स्त्रिया हळदीकुंकू करतात: मैत्रिणींना बोलावून हळद-कुंकू, भिजवलेले हरभरे, कैरीचे पन्हे, कैरीची डाळ आणि वाण दिले जाते.

summary.en: The birth of Rama, on the ninth day of bright Chaitra, at midday.

traditions.en: Temples and homes celebrate Rama's birth at midday, the hour he is said to have been born, with a small cradle holding an image of baby Rama rocked to songs. Many people fast until noon or through the day. The Ramayana or Ramcharitmanas is read, sometimes over all nine days of Navratri, finishing today. Processions (shobha yatras) carry images of Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and Hanuman through towns, and Ayodhya draws large crowds. Panakam (a jaggery and pepper drink) and kosambari are offered in the South, and in the North a sweet called panjiri is shared.

story.en: King Dasharatha of Ayodhya ruled well but had no children. On the advice of the sage Vasishtha, a great yajna was performed, and from its fire came a bowl of sweet payasam, which the king shared among his three queens. In time Kausalya gave birth to Rama on the ninth day of bright Chaitra, at midday; Kaikeyi to Bharata; and Sumitra to the twins Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Tradition remembers Rama as Maryada Purushottama, the one who kept to what was right even when it cost him most: he gave up his throne and went to the forest for fourteen years to keep his father's word. Ram Navami celebrates his birth and the life he went on to live.

en: Clean the puja space and decorate a small cradle or a picture of Rama with flowers.
Keep a fast through the morning if your family does; fruit and milk are usual.
Prepare panjiri, payasam or kheer, fruit and tulsi leaves for the offering.
Check the madhyahna (midday) time in the day view; that is the hour of Rama's birth.
At midday, light a lamp, rock the cradle gently, sing 'Bhaye prakat kripala' or another birth song, and offer the food.
Read a passage from the Ramayana or Ramcharitmanas, or listen to it together.
Share the prasad, break the fast with a simple meal, and join a local procession if there is one.

greeting.en: Jai Shri Ram! Warm wishes on Ram Navami.

summary.en: The birth of Hanuman, celebrated on Chaitra Purnima across North India.

traditions.en: Devotees visit Hanuman temples from early morning, since Hanuman is said to have been born at sunrise. The idol is offered sindoor mixed with jasmine oil, a garland of betel leaves, and boondi or besan laddoos. The Hanuman Chalisa is recited, often many times over, and the Sundarkand of the Ramcharitmanas is read. Many keep a fast for the day. Celebrations are large at Salasar Balaji in Rajasthan and in Hanuman temples across Uttar Pradesh. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala the day is kept in Margazhi, and in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana in Vaishakha.

story.en: Hanuman was born to Anjana and Kesari, and is called the son of Vayu, the wind, who watched over him. The story told of his childhood is that, seeing the rising Sun, he took it for a ripe fruit and leapt into the sky to catch it. Indra, alarmed, struck him with his thunderbolt, and the child fell, wounding his jaw (hanu), which gave him his name. Vayu, grieving, withdrew the air from the world until the gods came together to revive the child and gave him gifts of strength, wisdom and long life. Hanuman grew up to become Rama's devoted friend and messenger, who leapt across the ocean to find Sita in Lanka. He is remembered for strength used in service, and for humility.

en: Wake early and bathe before sunrise, the hour of Hanuman's birth.
Visit a Hanuman temple, or set up a picture of Hanuman at home with a red cloth.
Offer sindoor (or a little vermilion), a red flower garland, and boondi or besan laddoos.
Light a lamp with ghee or jasmine oil.
Recite the Hanuman Chalisa, once or as many times as you like; read the Sundarkand if you have time.
Keep a fast for the day if your family does, eating once in the evening.
Share the laddoos as prasad, and if you can, help someone who needs it, in Hanuman's spirit of service.

greeting.en: Jai Hanuman! Wishing you strength and a steady heart on Hanuman Jayanti.

summary.en: The third day of bright Vaishakha, traditionally favoured for new beginnings and for giving.

traditions.en: 'Akshaya' means 'that which does not diminish', and the day is traditionally seen as good for starting things: a business, a house, a course of study, a marriage. Many families buy a little gold or silver, and many more give: water and cooling drinks, fans, umbrellas, grain and clothes, since it falls in the hot season. Vishnu and Lakshmi are worshipped, and in Odisha the building of the chariots for the Puri Rath Yatra begins today. Parashurama Jayanti falls on or near the same day, and Jain families break the year-long varshi tapa fast with sugarcane juice.

story.en: Several stories meet on this day. In one, Krishna's childhood friend Sudama, a poor Brahmin, walked to Dwarka to see him, carrying only a little beaten rice (poha) tied in a cloth as a gift. Krishna embraced him, ate the poha with delight, and sent him home without Sudama asking for anything; when Sudama returned, his family's hardship had ended. In another, during the Pandavas' exile, Krishna gave Draupadi the Akshaya Patra, a vessel that never ran empty until she had eaten, so no guest at their door went hungry. Tradition also holds that the Treta Yuga began on this day, that the Ganga descended to earth, and that Vyasa began dictating the Mahabharata to Ganesha.

en: In the morning, bathe and offer a lamp, flowers and tulsi to Vishnu and Lakshmi at home.
Offer something simple and cooling: barley, sattu, cucumber, jaggery water or panakam.
If you were planning to start something, a course, a savings plan or a small venture, many families choose today to begin.
Give something in the spirit of the day: water or buttermilk to passers-by, an umbrella, a fan, grain or clothes.
If your family buys gold or silver, keep it small and meaningful; the giving matters more in the tradition.
Share a simple meal, and if you can, feed a guest or someone who needs it.

greeting.en: May what you begin today grow steadily. Happy Akshaya Tritiya!

summary.en: The Vat Savitri observance as kept on Jyeshtha Purnima in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Goa.

traditions.en: In Maharashtra, Gujarat, Goa and parts of Karnataka, married women keep the Vat Savitri observance on the full moon of Jyeshtha rather than on the new moon. They gather at a banyan tree in nine-yard saris, tie thread around it, offer mangoes, jackfruit and sweets, and exchange haldi-kumkum and vayan, small gifts, with one another.

story.en: The story is the same as Vat Savitri's: Savitri, who followed Yama when he came for her husband Satyavan beneath a banyan tree, and through her wisdom and persistence won him back. The banyan, with its roots that drop from its branches and become new trunks, is seen in this tradition as a picture of a long, sheltering life, which is why the observance is kept at its foot.

en: Fast from the morning if you can.
Take water, thread, haldi-kumkum, flowers, fruit and a sweet to a banyan tree.
Offer them at the roots and walk around the tree winding the thread.
Exchange haldi-kumkum and small gifts with the women gathered, and listen to the Savitri story.
Break the fast in the evening.

greeting.en: Happy Vat Purnima!

variations: The wari, the pilgrims' walk from Alandi and Dehu, reaches Pandharpur for the darshan of Vitthal on this day.

summary.en: Ashadha Shukla Ekadashi: Vishnu goes into his four-month yogic sleep; chaturmas begins.

traditions.en: Also called Ashadhi Ekadashi and Padma Ekadashi, it begins chaturmas, the four months of the monsoon when many people take on a discipline: giving up a food, eating once a day, or reading daily. In Maharashtra, the great Pandharpur Wari reaches its end: lakhs of warkaris walk for weeks, singing abhangs, to see Vitthal on this day. Traditionally, weddings and housewarmings are not held until Vishnu wakes on Devutthana Ekadashi.

story.en: The story told is that on this Ekadashi Vishnu lies down on the serpent Shesha in the ocean of milk and enters yoga nidra, a sleep of deep meditation, for four months, waking on Kartika Shukla Ekadashi. Another story, told in Maharashtra, is of Pundalik, a young man devoted to his parents. When Vishnu, as Vitthal, came to his door, Pundalik was massaging his father's feet, and without rising he tossed Vitthal a brick to stand on until he was done. Vitthal waited, standing on the brick with his hands on his hips, and stands that way in Pandharpur to this day.

en: Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu or Vitthal with tulsi and a lamp; sing abhangs or bhajans.
If you wish, choose a small discipline for the four months of chaturmas.
Join a local dindi or temple procession if there is one.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: The full moon of Ashadha, for honouring teachers, remembering Vyasa.

traditions.en: Students visit and thank their teachers, and disciples gather at ashrams and with their spiritual guides. Music and dance students offer flowers and a performance to their gurus. Many families honour parents and elders as their first teachers. Ashrams hold Vyasa puja, and the day begins the four months of chaturmas, when wandering monks stay in one place for the monsoon. Buddhists remember it as the day the Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath.

story.en: Guru Purnima is the birthday of Veda Vyasa, born to the sage Parashara and Satyavati on an island in the Yamuna. Tradition credits him with dividing the one Veda into four so that it could be learned, composing the Mahabharata, and compiling the Puranas, which is why he is honoured as the teacher of teachers and the day is also called Vyasa Purnima. Yogic tradition adds that on this full moon Shiva, the Adiyogi, sat facing south and began to teach the first seven disciples, the Saptarishis, becoming the first guru.

en: Think of the teachers who shaped you: at school, in music or a craft, at home, or on a spiritual path.
Visit or call one of them to thank them; take flowers, fruit or a small gift if you visit.
At home, light a lamp before a picture of Vyasa, your guru or your family deity, and offer flowers.
Touch the feet of your parents and elders, your first teachers.
Spend a little time studying or practising something you have learned, in your teacher's honour.

greeting.en: With gratitude to every teacher. Happy Guru Purnima!

summary.en: Shravana Shukla Panchami: the day of honouring serpents, guardians of the earth and water.

traditions.en: Families draw images of serpents with sandal paste, turmeric or cow dung on the walls or at the doorway, or worship stone nagas under trees and at temples, offering milk, turmeric, rice, flowers and durva. Many avoid digging the earth or cutting with sharp tools for the day. Women in Maharashtra and Karnataka sing traditional songs and swing on swings. Today, many communities rightly avoid giving milk to live snakes, which harms them, and offer it to stone images instead.

story.en: The serpents are honoured in many stories: Shesha, on whom Vishnu rests, Vasuki, who served as the rope in the churning of the ocean, and the nagas who guard springs and wells. One story told for this day is of Krishna, who as a boy overcame the serpent Kaliya in the Yamuna and danced on his hoods, then let him go to live in peace in the ocean. Another folk story is of a farmer who, ploughing, harmed a serpent's young without knowing; the farmer's daughter prayed to the serpent mother with milk and an apology, and the serpent forgave the family. The day is about respect for the creatures with whom farmers share the fields in the rainy season.

en: Draw a serpent image at the doorway with turmeric or sandal paste, or visit a naga shrine or temple.
Offer milk, turmeric, rice, flowers and durva grass to the image.
If your family does, avoid digging or cutting with sharp tools today.
Do not feed milk to live snakes; it harms them.
Listen to the Nag Panchami story and share sweets.

greeting.en: Wishes on Nag Panchami: respect for every living thing.

summary.en: Shravana Purnima on the Konkan coast: fishing communities offer a coconut to the sea as the monsoon season ends.
summary.mr: कोकण किनाऱ्यावरील श्रावण पौर्णिमा: पावसाळा संपत येताना कोळी समाज समुद्राला नारळ अर्पण करतो.

traditions.en: The Koli fishing community, and coastal Maharashtra with them, decorate their boats, carry a gilded coconut to the shore in procession with music and dance, and offer it to the sea, thanking it and marking the start of the new fishing season. Narali bhat, sweet coconut rice, is cooked at home. The same day is Raksha Bandhan.
traditions.mr: कोळी समाज आणि त्यांच्यासोबत किनारपट्टीवरील महाराष्ट्र होड्या सजवतो, सोनेरी कागदात मढवलेला नारळ वाजतगाजत मिरवणुकीने किनाऱ्यावर नेतो आणि समुद्राला अर्पण करतो, कृतज्ञता व्यक्त करत नवा मासेमारीचा हंगाम सुरू करतो. घरी नारळीभात केला जातो. याच दिवशी रक्षाबंधनही असते.

summary.en: Shravana Purnima: sisters tie a rakhi on their brothers' wrists, and brothers promise to stand by them.

traditions.en: In the morning sisters prepare a thali with a rakhi, roli, rice, a lamp and sweets. They apply a tilak to their brother's forehead, tie the rakhi on his right wrist, wave the lamp and feed him a sweet; the brother gives a gift and a promise of support. Cousins and friends tie rakhis too, and sisters far away post them. Rakhi is tied outside the Bhadra period, which the day view shows. In Maharashtra the same full moon is Narali Purnima, when fishing communities offer coconuts to the sea, and in the South it is Avani Avittam, when the sacred thread is renewed.

story.en: Many stories are told. In the Mahabharata, Krishna cut his finger, and Draupadi tore a strip from her sari to bind it; Krishna promised to repay the kindness, and did so when he protected her honour in the Kaurava court. In another, the asura king Bali had kept Vishnu as his doorkeeper, and Lakshmi, wanting him home, tied a thread on Bali's wrist as a sister and asked for her husband back as her gift; Bali gladly agreed. A story from history tells of Rani Karnavati of Mewar sending a rakhi to the emperor Humayun to ask for help. In all of them, the thread is a promise of care between people who choose to stand by one another.

en: Choose rakhis, and buy or make sweets the day before; post rakhis early for siblings far away.
Check the day view for the Bhadra period, and plan the ceremony after it ends.
Prepare a thali: rakhi, roli or kumkum, rice, a small lamp and sweets.
The brother sits facing east; the sister applies a tilak, tilts a few grains of rice on it, and ties the rakhi on his right wrist.
She waves the lamp, feeds him a sweet, and he gives her a gift and his blessing or promise.
Call or video-call siblings you cannot meet, and share a meal with the family.

greeting.en: Happy Raksha Bandhan to every brother and sister!

summary.en: The birth of Krishna, kept with a fast and a midnight celebration.

traditions.en: Devotees fast through the day and gather at midnight, the hour of Krishna's birth, to bathe an image of baby Krishna (Laddu Gopal) in milk and curd, dress him and rock him in a decorated cradle while singing bhajans. Homes and temples set up jhankis, scenes from his life, and children dress up as Krishna and Radha. Mathura and Vrindavan celebrate for days. In Maharashtra, the next day is Dahi Handi, when human pyramids climb to break pots of curd hung high, as young Krishna stole butter. The fast is broken after midnight with makhan-mishri and panjiri.

story.en: King Kamsa of Mathura was told that the eighth child of his sister Devaki would end his rule, so he imprisoned her and her husband Vasudeva. Krishna was born at midnight in that prison, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, under Rohini nakshatra, in a storm. The story goes that the guards fell asleep and the chains and doors opened. Vasudeva carried the baby in a basket through the flooded Yamuna, which parted for them, with the serpent Shesha spreading his hoods over the child against the rain. In Gokul he exchanged Krishna for the newborn daughter of Nanda and Yashoda, who raised Krishna as their own. He grew up among the cowherds, beloved for his mischief, his flute, and his care for everyone around him.

en: Decorate a small cradle and set up an image of baby Krishna (Laddu Gopal); make a jhanki if you like.
Fast through the day: many take fruit and milk; elders and children often keep it light.
Prepare panchamrit (milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar), makhan-mishri, panjiri and tulsi leaves.
Sing bhajans and read the story of Krishna's birth in the evening.
Check the day view for the Nishita time around midnight; at that moment bathe the image with panchamrit, dress it and place it in the cradle.
Rock the cradle, sing 'Nand ke anand bhayo', and offer the food and tulsi.
Share the prasad and break the fast.

greeting.en: Jai Shri Krishna! Happy Janmashtami.

summary.en: The day after Gokulashtami: Dahi Handi, when human pyramids break a pot of curd hung high above the street.
summary.mr: गोकुळाष्टमीचा दुसरा दिवस: दहीहंडी, उंच टांगलेली दह्याची हंडी मानवी मनोरे रचून फोडली जाते.

traditions.en: Recalling young Krishna and his friends stealing butter from pots hung out of reach, teams of govindas form human pyramids, sometimes many tiers high, to break a handi of curd, buttermilk and coins strung over the street, while crowds sing and splash water. At home and in temples, gopalkala, a dish of poha, curd, cucumber and pickle, is offered and shared.
traditions.mr: उंच टांगलेल्या मडक्यांतून लोणी चोरणाऱ्या बाळकृष्णाच्या आठवणीत गोविंदा पथके मानवी मनोरे रचून रस्त्यावर टांगलेली दही, ताक आणि नाणी असलेली हंडी फोडतात, तर गर्दी गाणी गाते आणि पाणी उडवते. घरी व मंदिरांत पोहे, दही, काकडी आणि लोणचे घालून केलेला गोपाळकाला नैवेद्य म्हणून दाखवून वाटला जातो.

summary.en: Shravana Amavasya: Bail Pola, the farmers' festival honouring the bullocks that work their fields.
summary.mr: श्रावण अमावास्या: बैलपोळा, शेतात राबणाऱ्या बैलांचा सन्मान करणारा शेतकऱ्यांचा सण.

traditions.en: The bullocks rest from work. They are bathed, their horns painted, their bodies decorated with colours, bells, garlands and embroidered cloths (jhul), and they are fed puran poli. In the afternoon they are led in procession through the village to the temple, and the farmer's family performs their aarti. Children in towns play with clay or wooden bullocks.
traditions.mr: बैलांना कामातून विश्रांती दिली जाते. त्यांना अंघोळ घालून शिंगे रंगवली जातात, अंगावर रंग, घुंगरमाळा, हार आणि झूल घातली जाते आणि पुरणपोळी खाऊ घातली जाते. दुपारी गावातून त्यांची मिरवणूक मंदिरापर्यंत निघते आणि शेतकऱ्याचे कुटुंब त्यांची आरती करते. शहरांत मुले मातीच्या किंवा लाकडी बैलांशी खेळतात.

summary.en: Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya: a strict fast remembering how Parvati's friends helped her keep her vow for Shiva.

traditions.en: Women, married and unmarried, keep a strict fast, many without water, from sunrise until the next morning. Clay or sand images of Shiva, Parvati and Parvati's friend are made and worshipped at dusk with bel leaves, flowers and the sixteen adornments. Women stay awake through the night singing bhajans, and the images are immersed the next morning before the fast is broken. It is widely kept in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Nepal.

story.en: 'Hartalika' joins 'harat', taken away, and 'aalika', friend. Parvati had set her heart on Shiva, but her father Himavan promised her to Vishnu. Her friends, seeing her distress, took her away into the forest, where she made a linga of sand and kept a fast and night-long worship for Shiva on Bhadrapada Shukla Tritiya. Shiva, moved by her resolve, appeared and agreed to marry her, and her father, learning of it, gave his blessing. The festival honours both Parvati's determination and her friends' loyalty.

en: Decide how you will fast; those with health conditions often keep it with water or fruit.
Make or buy small clay images of Shiva and Parvati, and gather bel leaves, flowers, and adornments such as bangles and sindoor.
At dusk, set up the images, light a lamp and worship them, listening to the Hartalika story.
Keep a night vigil with bhajans if you can.
The next morning, worship again, immerse the images in water, and break the fast.

greeting.en: Wishes on Hartalika Teej to every woman keeping the vrat.

summary.en: Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturthi: Ganesha's birthday, welcomed home for up to ten days.

traditions.en: Families bring home a clay image of Ganesha and install it at midday with the pranapratishtha prayer, and many neighbourhoods set up large public pandals. Ganesha is offered modaks, durva grass, red flowers and the 21 leaves of the patri puja, with aartis morning and evening. Homes keep him for one and a half, three, five, seven or ten days, then carry him in procession to water for immersion (visarjan) with the cry 'Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya!' (come again soon next year). Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh celebrate most grandly. Tradition asks that the Moon not be looked at on this night.

story.en: Parvati, it is said, made a boy from the turmeric paste she used for her bath, breathed life into him, and set him to guard her door. When Shiva came home, the boy, who did not know him, would not let him in, and in the struggle that followed Shiva struck off the boy's head. Parvati's grief was so great that Shiva promised to restore him, and sent his attendants to bring the head of the first creature they found facing north. They returned with an elephant's head, and Shiva set it on the boy and brought him back to life, naming him Ganapati, lord of his ganas, and declaring that he would be worshipped first before every undertaking. The Moon, it is told, laughed at Ganesha's round belly that night, and so the Moon is not looked at on Ganesh Chaturthi.

en: Choose an eco-friendly clay image; decorate a small platform (mandap) with flowers and lights.
Prepare modaks or laddoos, durva grass, red flowers and a lamp.
At madhyahna (midday; see the day view), install Ganesha with a prayer inviting him into the image, and offer the durva, flowers and modaks.
Perform aarti morning and evening for as many days as your family keeps him.
On the day of visarjan, do a final aarti, carry Ganesha to water, or immerse him at home in a bucket and pour the water on plants.
Avoid looking at the Moon on the night of Chaturthi, as tradition asks.

greeting.en: Ganpati Bappa Morya! Happy Ganesh Chaturthi.

summary.en: Bhadrapada Shukla Panchami: honouring the seven sages, the Saptarishis.

traditions.en: Women, especially, keep a fast and bathe with special care, traditionally with the herb apamarga, and worship the seven sages, Kashyapa, Atri, Bharadvaja, Vishvamitra, Gautama, Jamadagni and Vasishtha, together with Arundhati. Many eat only food that grows without ploughing on this day. It is kept mainly in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nepal and parts of North India.

story.en: The Saptarishis are remembered as the seers who first heard the Vedas in meditation and passed them on, and as the stars of the Great Bear, circling the pole star. The day honours them as the source of the knowledge families have handed down. Arundhati, Vasishtha's wife, is worshipped with them as the model of a companion in learning, and her faint star beside Vasishtha's is shown to couples at their weddings.

en: Bathe in the morning; if your family does, with apamarga leaves.
Draw or place seven betel nuts or small images for the seven sages and Arundhati on a clean cloth.
Offer flowers, sandal paste, fruit and a lamp, and recite their names.
Eat simple food that grows without ploughing, such as fruit or wild rice, if you keep the custom.

greeting.en: With respect to the seven sages, wishes on Rishi Panchami.

summary.en: The Anuradha star in Bhadrapada: Gauri (Mahalakshmi) arrives in Maharashtrian homes during Ganeshotsav.
summary.mr: भाद्रपदातील अनुराधा नक्षत्र: गणेशोत्सवात गौरी (महालक्ष्मी) घरी येतात.

traditions.en: Gauri comes for three days, welcomed on Anuradha, worshipped on Jyeshtha and bid farewell on Mula. Women carry her, often as two figures (Jyeshtha and Kanishtha), from the door to her seat, leaving kumkum footprints and naming each room as they pass. She is dressed in a saree and jewellery and seated beside Ganesha.
traditions.mr: गौरी तीन दिवसांसाठी येतात: अनुराधेवर आवाहन, ज्येष्ठेवर पूजन आणि मुळावर विसर्जन. स्त्रिया गौरींना, बहुधा ज्येष्ठा-कनिष्ठा अशा दोन रूपांत, दारापासून त्यांच्या आसनापर्यंत आणतात; कुंकवाची पावले उमटवतात आणि प्रत्येक खोली दाखवत जातात. त्यांना साडी, दागिने घालून गणपतीशेजारी बसवले जाते.

summary.en: The Jyeshtha star in Bhadrapada: the main day of Gauri's visit, with a feast of sixteen dishes.
summary.mr: भाद्रपदातील ज्येष्ठा नक्षत्र: गौरी आगमनाचा मुख्य दिवस, सोळा भाज्यांचा नैवेद्य.

traditions.en: Gauri is offered a grand naivedya: puran poli, sixteen vegetables, ambil, karanji and laddoos. Women of the neighbourhood are invited for haldi-kunku, and in the evening there are aartis and songs.
traditions.mr: गौरींना मोठा नैवेद्य दाखवला जातो: पुरणपोळी, सोळा भाज्या, आंबिल, करंज्या आणि लाडू. शेजारच्या स्त्रियांना हळदीकुंकवासाठी बोलावले जाते आणि संध्याकाळी आरत्या व गाणी होतात.

summary.en: The Mula star in Bhadrapada: Gauri is bid farewell after her three-day visit.
summary.mr: भाद्रपदातील मूळ नक्षत्र: तीन दिवसांच्या मुक्कामानंतर गौरींचे विसर्जन.

traditions.en: After a final aarti and an offering of curd-rice, the Gauris are given leave; in many homes their faces are taken to water, and in others a symbolic farewell is made and the figures stored for next year. Women tie a thread blessed during the worship.
traditions.mr: शेवटची आरती आणि दहीभाताचा नैवेद्य झाल्यावर गौरींना निरोप दिला जातो; अनेक घरी मुखवटे पाण्यात विसर्जित होतात, तर काही घरी प्रतीकात्मक निरोप देऊन ते पुढच्या वर्षासाठी ठेवले जातात. पूजेत ठेवलेला दोरा स्त्रिया बांधतात.

summary.en: Bhadrapada Shukla Chaturdashi: worship of Vishnu as Ananta, and the last day of Ganeshotsav.

traditions.en: Families worship Vishnu as Ananta, the endless, and tie an anant sutra, a thread with fourteen knots dyed with turmeric, on the arm: men on the right, women on the left. Many keep a fast and eat salt-free food. In Maharashtra and wherever Ganeshotsav is celebrated for ten days, this is the day of the grand visarjan processions, with drums, dancing and huge crowds seeing Ganesha off to the sea and lakes.

story.en: The story told is of Sushila, daughter of a sage, who saw women worshipping Ananta by a river and joined them, tying the fourteen-knotted thread on her arm. Her husband Kaundinya, not knowing what it was, threw it into the fire, and from then on their life fell into difficulty. Realising his mistake, he set out to find Ananta and wandered until an old Brahmin led him to a cave and revealed himself as Vishnu. Kaundinya kept the observance for fourteen years, and the family's life was steadied. The fourteen knots are said to stand for the fourteen worlds Vishnu sustains. In the Mahabharata, Krishna tells this story to Yudhishthira during the Pandavas' exile.

en: Prepare an anant sutra: a cotton or silk thread with fourteen knots, dyed with turmeric.
Set up a picture of Vishnu, place the thread before him, and offer flowers, tulsi and a sweet.
Hear the Ananta story, then tie the thread on the arm.
If Ganesha is with you for ten days, do the final aarti and take him for visarjan.

greeting.en: Wishes on Anant Chaturdashi. Ganpati Bappa Morya!

summary.en: Mahalaya Amavasya: the last day of Pitru Paksha, for remembering all ancestors.

traditions.en: This new moon is for remembering all ancestors, including those whose tithi is not known, and anyone in the family who has no one else to remember them. Families offer tarpan and shraddha at rivers and at home, feed people and give generously. In Bengal, the dawn of Mahalaya is greeted with the radio recitation of Mahishasura Mardini, and the day marks the Goddess's journey toward the Durga Puja that follows.

story.en: As the last day of the fortnight that Karna was granted, this new moon gathers in everyone the family wishes to remember. Tradition says the ancestors, having visited their descendants through Pitru Paksha, return on this day, and the offerings made now accompany them. In Bengal, the day is also the 'devi paksha' threshold: the Goddess begins her journey to her parents' home, and the next day Navratri begins.

en: At aparahna, the afternoon (see the day view), offer water with black sesame, facing south, for all your ancestors, naming those you know.
Cook a simple meal and offer a portion to crows, cows or dogs.
Feed someone or give grain, clothes or a meal to those in need.
Light a lamp in the evening in their memory.

greeting.en: Remembering all who came before us, on Mahalaya.

summary.en: Nine nights of the Goddess in Ashvin, ending in Dussehra.

traditions.en: On the first morning families set up the kalash (ghatasthapana) and sow barley, and for nine days worship one form of Durga each day: Shailaputri, Brahmacharini, Chandraghanta, Kushmanda, Skandamata, Katyayani, Kalaratri, Mahagauri and Siddhidatri. Many fast or eat only vrat food. Evenings bring garba and dandiya in Gujarat, Ram Lila plays across the North, and the grand Durga Puja pandals of Bengal in the last five days. On Ashtami or Navami, young girls are honoured as the Goddess in kanya puja.

story.en: The Devi Mahatmya tells that the buffalo-demon Mahishasura, granted a boon that no man or god could defeat him, drove the gods from heaven. The gods' anger and strength combined into a blaze of light from which the Goddess Durga took form, and each god gave her a weapon: Shiva his trident, Vishnu his discus, Indra his thunderbolt. Riding a lion, she fought Mahishasura for nine days and nights as he changed shape again and again, and on the tenth day she overcame him. Navratri keeps those nine nights, and Vijayadashami celebrates the victory.

en: The day before, clean the puja space and gather a kalash, coconut, mango leaves, barley and soil.
On the first morning, set up the kalash and sow barley beside it; light a lamp before the Goddess.
Each day, worship that day's form of Durga with flowers and an aarti, and read a portion of the Durga Saptashati if you can.
Choose your fast: one meal, fruit and milk, or vrat foods like kuttu, singhara and sabudana.
In the evenings, join a garba, a Ram Lila or a Durga Puja pandal.
On Ashtami or Navami, invite young girls home, wash their feet, and serve them puri, chana and halwa with a small gift.

greeting.en: Jai Mata Di! Wishing you a joyful Navratri.

summary.en: Vijayadashami: Rama's victory over Ravana and Durga's over Mahishasura.

traditions.en: Across North India, the Ram Lila ends with huge effigies of Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Meghnad set alight at dusk, to cheers and fireworks. In Bengal, Durga is bid farewell with sindoor khela and immersion. In Mysuru, a grand procession is held. Many people worship the shami tree and exchange its leaves (or apta leaves in Maharashtra) as 'gold'. The day is traditionally favoured for beginning things, especially learning, and children in the South begin their letters (Vidyarambham).

story.en: In the Ramayana, Ravana carried Sita away to Lanka. Rama, with Lakshmana, Hanuman and the army of the vanaras, built a bridge across the sea and fought a long war. Before the final battle Rama worshipped the Goddess for nine days, and on the tenth he defeated Ravana and freed Sita. The same day is remembered as Durga's victory over Mahishasura. In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas, at the end of their exile, took down the weapons they had hidden in a shami tree on this day.

en: In the morning, worship Rama and the Goddess, and conclude Navratri; immerse or set aside the sprouted barley.
At aparahna (afternoon; see the day view), worship the shami tree if there is one nearby.
Exchange shami or apta leaves with family and friends as a token of goodwill.
In the evening, watch the Ravana dahan at a local Ram Lila.
If a child is starting school or learning, help them write their first letters today.

greeting.en: Happy Dussehra! May every good effort of yours find its victory.

summary.en: The autumn full moon of Ashvin: kheer under the moonlight, and Kojagari Lakshmi worship.

traditions.en: On the brightest full moon of the year, families cook rice kheer and leave it out in the moonlight for some hours, then eat it as prasad. Many stay awake into the night, singing and playing games, and in Bengal and Odisha Lakshmi is worshipped as Kojagari Lakshmi. In Braj, the night is remembered as the night of Krishna's Raas Leela with the gopis.

story.en: 'Kojagari' comes from 'ko jagarti', who is awake? The story told is that on this night Lakshmi walks the earth asking that question, and visits the homes where people are awake and lamps are lit. Braj tradition remembers it as the night Krishna played his flute in the forest and the gopis came to dance the Maha Raas with him, each feeling that Krishna danced with her alone. The moon is said to be full in all sixteen of its kalas, and its light especially gentle, which is why the kheer is left out to take it in.

en: Cook rice kheer in the evening.
After moonrise, cover it with a thin cloth and leave it on a terrace or balcony in the moonlight for a few hours.
Light lamps and worship Lakshmi, or Radha-Krishna, with flowers and an aarti.
Stay up with family for a while, then share the kheer as prasad.

greeting.en: Wishing you a bright, peaceful Sharad Purnima.

summary.en: Ashvin Krishna Dvadashi, the first day of Diwali in Maharashtra: cows and calves are honoured.
summary.mr: आश्विन कृष्ण द्वादशी, महाराष्ट्रात दिवाळीचा पहिला दिवस: गाय-वासराची पूजा.

traditions.en: In the evening women worship a cow and her calf with haldi-kunku, flowers and a lamp, and feed them bajra bhakri and gavar or other greens; many avoid wheat and milk products for the day out of regard for the cow. Lamps are lit for the first time that Diwali, and the season's first rangoli is drawn.
traditions.mr: संध्याकाळी स्त्रिया गाय-वासराची हळद-कुंकू, फुले आणि दिव्याने पूजा करतात आणि त्यांना बाजरीची भाकरी व गवारीची भाजी खाऊ घालतात; गाईच्या सन्मानार्थ अनेक जणी दिवसभर गहू आणि दूधजन्य पदार्थ टाळतात. दिवाळीचे पहिले दिवे लागतात आणि पहिली रांगोळी काढली जाते.

summary.en: Dhanatrayodashi, the first day of Diwali: Dhanvantari's day, and a day for new utensils and lamps.

traditions.en: Homes are cleaned and decorated, rangoli is drawn at the door, and many families buy a new utensil, a coin, or something of gold or silver. In the evening Lakshmi and Kubera are worshipped, and a lamp is lit for Yama outside the house facing south, a custom called Yam Deepdaan. Ayurvedic practitioners honour Dhanvantari, and the day is also observed as National Ayurveda Day.

story.en: In the churning of the ocean, Dhanvantari, the physician of the gods and the teacher of Ayurveda, rose from the waters on this day holding a pot of amrit. That is why the day is 'Dhan-teras': the thirteenth day of Dhanvantari. Another story tells of King Hima's son, whose stars foretold he would die four days after his wedding. On that night his young wife laid all her jewellery and coins in a heap at the door, lit lamps everywhere, and kept him awake with stories and songs. When Yama came as a serpent, he was dazzled by the light and the gold, sat on the heap listening to her songs, and left at dawn without taking the prince. The lamp lit for Yama tonight remembers her.

en: Finish cleaning the house, and draw a rangoli at the entrance.
If your family does, buy a new steel or brass utensil, a coin, or a small piece of silver or gold.
At pradosh (dusk; see the day view), worship Lakshmi, Kubera and Dhanvantari with lamps, flowers and sweets.
Light a four-wicked lamp outside the house facing south for Yam Deepdaan.
Light lamps at the doorway and windows for the evening.

greeting.en: Happy Dhanteras! Health and good things to your home.

summary.en: Choti Diwali: Krishna's victory over Narakasura, kept with an early oil bath and lamps.

traditions.en: Before dawn, families take an abhyanga snan, a bath after rubbing the body with oil and ubtan (a paste of gram flour, turmeric and herbs). Lamps are lit in the evening, and in some homes a small lamp is placed at the rubbish heap or drain, so no corner is left dark. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala this is Deepavali itself, celebrated with the dawn oil bath, new clothes and crackers. In the North it is called Choti Diwali, the eve of the main festival.

story.en: Narakasura, king of Pragjyotisha, had grown so powerful that he imprisoned sixteen thousand women and seized the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods. Krishna rode out against him with Satyabhama, and in some tellings it is Satyabhama herself who defeats him, since a boon said only his mother could end his life, and Satyabhama is remembered as an incarnation of Bhudevi, his mother. As he fell, Narakasura asked that the day be remembered with lights and joy, and Krishna granted it. Krishna then freed the imprisoned women and, so that none of them would be shunned, gave them the honour of his name.

en: Wake before dawn; rub sesame oil and then ubtan on your skin, and bathe.
Wear fresh or new clothes, and offer a prayer to Krishna.
In the evening, light lamps at the door, in every room and at the corners of the house.
Make or finish sweets for the next day, and finish decorating.

greeting.en: Happy Choti Diwali! May light reach every corner.

summary.en: Kartika Amavasya: the festival of lights, with Lakshmi Puja at dusk.

traditions.en: Homes are filled with diyas and lights, the doorway is marked with rangoli and small footprints of Lakshmi, and families wear new clothes. At dusk, Lakshmi and Ganesha are worshipped together, with account books and cash boxes blessed in business families. Sweets and dry fruits are exchanged with neighbours and relatives, and the evening is lit with lamps and fireworks. For Jains it marks Mahavira's nirvana, and for Sikhs it is Bandi Chhor Divas.

story.en: Diwali remembers Rama's return to Ayodhya after fourteen years of exile and his victory in Lanka. The people of Ayodhya, overjoyed, lit rows of lamps (deepavali) along every street on the dark new-moon night to welcome Rama, Sita and Lakshmana home. Lakshmi, who rose from the churning of the ocean and chose Vishnu, is worshipped on this night as the goddess of wellbeing and abundance, together with Ganesha, the remover of obstacles, so that every beginning in the new season is made well.

en: In the days before, clean the house thoroughly, and buy diyas, wicks, oil, flowers and sweets.
In the afternoon, draw a rangoli at the entrance and set out lamps.
Check the Lakshmi Puja time in the day view (pradosh, after sunset).
Set up Lakshmi and Ganesha on a red cloth, with a kalash, coins, rice, flowers, sweets and a lamp; worship them together, Ganesha first.
After the puja, light diyas at the door, windows, balcony and every room.
Share sweets with family and neighbours; if you light crackers, choose quieter ones and keep them away from children and animals.

greeting.en: Happy Diwali! May every lamp tonight bring light and warmth to your home.

summary.en: Kartika Shukla Pratipada, when Karnataka welcomes King Bali home for a day.

traditions.en: The day after Deepavali's Amavasya, homes draw rangoli of Bali and his kingdom, and in many villages an image of Bali is made from cow dung, decorated with flowers and worshipped at the doorway. Families light lamps, cattle are bathed and decorated, and in some homes it is the start of the new year in business accounts. It is the third and closing day of Deepavali in Karnataka.

story.en: The story told is of Bali, the generous king whose rule was so just that the gods grew uneasy. Vishnu came as Vamana, a small boy, and asked for three steps of land; Bali granted it, and Vamana's steps covered earth and sky and, with the third, Bali himself. Moved by his generosity, Vishnu let him return to his people one day each year, and Bali Padyami is that homecoming.

en: Draw a rangoli of Bali at the doorway, or make his image as is done locally.
Worship Bali with flowers and light lamps in the evening.
Bathe and decorate the cattle, and share the festive meal.

greeting.en: Happy Bali Padyami!

summary.en: Kartika Shukla Dwitiya: sisters welcome their brothers home, the last day of Diwali.

traditions.en: Brothers visit their sisters' homes, where the sister applies a tilak to his forehead, waves a lamp, feeds him sweets and a meal she has cooked, and prays for his long life; he gives her a gift. It is Bhau Beej in Maharashtra, Bhai Phonta in Bengal and Bhai Tika in Nepal. Sisters who cannot meet their brothers pray for them, and many call or video-call.

story.en: The story told is of Yamuna and her brother Yama. Yamuna had long asked her brother to visit, but he was always busy. On Kartika Shukla Dwitiya he finally came. Delighted, she welcomed him with a tilak and an aarti, cooked his favourite food and fed him with her own hands. Moved, Yama asked what she wished for, and she asked that every brother who visits his sister on this day and receives her tilak be blessed with a long life. Yama granted it, and the day is also called Yama Dwitiya.

en: Invite your brother home, or plan to visit your sister; call siblings who are far away.
Prepare a thali with roli, rice, a lamp, sweets and a coconut or dry fruit.
At aparahna (afternoon; see the day view), seat your brother, apply the tilak, wave the lamp and feed him a sweet.
Serve a meal you have cooked; the brother gives a gift and his blessing.

greeting.en: Happy Bhai Dooj to every brother and sister!

summary.en: Kartika Shukla Dwadashi: the wedding of the tulsi plant to Vishnu, opening the wedding season.

traditions.en: Families decorate the tulsi plant in the courtyard as a bride, with a red sari or cloth, bangles and a small canopy of sugarcane, and conduct a full wedding to Vishnu as Shaligram or to an image of Krishna, with mantras, garlands and the circling of the plant. Sweets are shared as at a wedding. Coming the day after Vishnu wakes from his four-month sleep, it is traditionally seen as the start of the season for weddings.

story.en: The story told is of Vrinda, a woman of great virtue married to the asura Jalandhara, whose strength came from her devotion. In the long conflict between Jalandhara and the gods, Vishnu took Jalandhara's form and came to Vrinda, and her vow was broken; Jalandhara fell. Grieving and angry, Vrinda declared that Vishnu would become a stone, and he became the Shaligram. She gave up her life, and from where she rested a tulsi plant grew. Moved by her devotion, Vishnu declared that he would always be honoured with tulsi, and that he would marry her each year in her plant form. Tulsi Vivah keeps that promise.

en: Clean and decorate the tulsi pot; build a small canopy with sugarcane stalks.
Dress the tulsi with a red cloth, bangles and a little sindoor, and place a Shaligram or image of Krishna beside her.
In the evening, perform the wedding: offer flowers, sweets and a garland, tie the two with a thread and walk around the plant.
Share sweets and the prasad as at a wedding.

greeting.en: Happy Tulsi Vivah!

summary.en: The full moon of Kartika: Dev Deepawali in Varanasi, Guru Nanak Jayanti, and the end of the holy month.

traditions.en: Kartika, a month of early baths and lamps, ends today. People bathe at dawn in rivers and lakes, and in the evening lamps are lit everywhere: in Varanasi the ghats glow with lakhs of diyas for Dev Deepawali, the gods' own Diwali. Lamps are floated on water. Sikhs celebrate Guru Nanak's birth (Gurpurab) with prabhat pheris, kirtan and langar. The Pushkar fair in Rajasthan reaches its peak, and in Odisha Boita Bandana sees small paper boats set sail.

story.en: The day is remembered as Tripuri Purnima: the three flying cities of the asura Tripurasura had been conquering the worlds, and could be struck only when, once in a thousand years, they aligned. On this full moon Shiva, with a single arrow from a bow that was Mount Meru, struck all three at once, and the gods, relieved, lit lamps in celebration: Dev Deepawali. Tradition also holds that Vishnu's first avatar, Matsya, the fish, appeared on Kartika Purnima to save Manu and the seeds of life from the great flood.

en: Bathe at dawn, in a river if you can.
Worship Vishnu or Shiva with flowers and a lamp; read the Satyanarayan katha if your family does.
At dusk, light many lamps at home, and float a lamp on water if you are near a river or lake.
Give food or a lamp to someone, and if you are Sikh or wish to join, visit a gurdwara for Gurpurab.

greeting.en: Wishes on Kartik Purnima and Dev Deepawali. May your home glow with light.

summary.en: Margazhi-month Sashti, a Murugan observance especially kept in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.

traditions.en: Devotees fast and worship Murugan, often in his serpent form as Subrahmanya, with milk, flowers and panchamritam. At Kukke Subramanya in Karnataka and at Murugan temples in Tamil Nadu, there are special abhishekams and processions. Many recite the Kanda Shashti Kavacham.

story.en: Tradition holds that on this Sashti Murugan, having overcome the asura Tarakasura, came to rest at Kukke, where the serpent king Vasuki was keeping tapas for his protection, and Murugan gave him shelter. He is worshipped there as Subrahmanya, the protector of the serpents.

en: Keep a fast or a simple vegetarian meal if your family does.
Worship Murugan with milk, flowers and panchamritam, and light a lamp.
Recite the Kanda Shashti Kavacham.

greeting.en: Subrahmanya Sashti greetings.

summary.en: Margashirsha Purnima: the birth of Dattatreya, in whom Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are joined.

traditions.en: Dattatreya is worshipped at dusk, the hour of his birth, especially in Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, at Ganagapur, Narsobawadi and Audumbar. Devotees read the Guru Charitra over the preceding days, sing bhajans, and offer flowers and sweets. He is often pictured with three heads, six arms, a cow and four dogs, beneath an audumbar (fig) tree.

story.en: Anasuya, wife of the sage Atri, was so renowned for her devotion that the goddesses Saraswati, Lakshmi and Parvati asked their husbands to test her. Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva came to her ashram as wandering monks and asked for food, but only if she served them unclothed. Anasuya, by the power of her devotion, turned the three into infants, and fed and cared for them as their mother. When the goddesses came seeking their husbands, she restored them, and the three gods, pleased, offered her a boon. She asked that they be born as her son, and so Dattatreya, 'given' (datta) to Atri, was born, uniting all three.

en: Read a chapter of the Guru Charitra or Dattatreya stotras in the morning.
At dusk, set up a picture of Dattatreya, light a lamp and offer flowers, tulsi and a sweet.
Sing a Datta bhajan such as 'Digambara Digambara Shripad Vallabh Digambara'.
Feed a cow or a dog if you can, and share the prasad.

greeting.en: Wishes on Dattatreya Jayanti.

summary.en: Chaitra Shukla Ekadashi, the first Ekadashi of the new year.

traditions.en: As with every Ekadashi, devotees of Vishnu fast from grains and beans, many on fruit and milk, spend time in prayer and break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi. Coming just after Rama Navami, Kamada Ekadashi is often kept with readings from the Ramayana and the singing of Vishnu's names.

story.en: The story told is of Lalit and Lalita, a gandharva couple at the court of King Pundarika. Lalit, distracted by thoughts of his wife, sang out of tune before the king, and the king in his anger declared that he would take the form of a fearsome rakshasa. Lalita followed her husband through the forests, caring for him, until she met the sage Shringi, who told her of the Ekadashi of Chaitra. She kept the fast with full devotion and offered its merit to her husband, and Lalit was restored to his own form. The two returned home together.

en: The evening before (Dashami), eat a light meal without grains in the night.
On Ekadashi, fast from grains and beans; take fruit, milk and nuts, or keep a stricter fast if you are able.
Worship Vishnu with tulsi, flowers and a lamp, and read or listen to the day's story.
Chant Vishnu's names or the Vishnu Sahasranama, and keep the day calm.
Break the fast the next morning within the Dvadashi time, with simple food.

summary.en: Vaishakha Krishna Ekadashi (Chaitra in the amanta reckoning), the Ekadashi of protection.

traditions.en: Devotees fast and worship Vishnu in his Vamana form. Tradition especially values giving on this day: food, water in the summer heat, and help to students. Many avoid honey, meat, betel and gambling, and keep the day quiet.

story.en: The story told is of King Mandhata, a just and generous ruler on the banks of the Narmada, who was absorbed in tapas when a bear attacked him and dragged him into the forest. He did not abandon his calm, but prayed to Vishnu, who came and freed him; but the king's foot was badly injured. Vishnu told him to keep the Varuthini Ekadashi at Mathura and worship his Varaha form, and the king, keeping the observance, was made whole. 'Varuthini' means 'the one that shields', and the day is remembered as a time of shelter.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans; fruit and milk are usual.
Worship Vishnu with tulsi and a lamp, and hear the story of King Mandhata.
Give water, food or help to someone, in the spirit of the day.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Vaishakha Shukla Ekadashi, named for Vishnu's Mohini form.

traditions.en: Devotees fast and worship Vishnu, remembering the form in which he appeared during the churning of the ocean. In temples, especially in Gujarat and the South, the deity is adorned as Mohini. The day is kept with prayer, reading and singing of Vishnu's names.

story.en: When the gods and asuras churned the ocean and the pot of amrit rose, the asuras seized it. Vishnu took the form of Mohini, an enchanting woman, and offered to share the nectar fairly; captivated, the asuras agreed, and Mohini served it to the gods. The day also carries the story of Dhrishtabuddhi, a merchant's son who wasted his inheritance and lost his way, until the sage Kaundinya told him of this Ekadashi. He kept it sincerely, and his life turned toward steadiness and kindness.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu with tulsi, yellow flowers and a lamp; hear the story of the churning and of Dhrishtabuddhi.
Spend time in prayer or reading, and avoid harsh speech.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Jyeshtha Krishna Ekadashi (Vaishakha in the amanta reckoning), also called Achala Ekadashi.

traditions.en: 'Apara' means boundless. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu as Trivikrama, the form that measured the worlds in three steps. In Odisha the day is called Jalakrida Ekadashi, and in Punjab and Haryana, Bhadrakali Ekadashi. As the summer heat peaks, giving water and cooling drinks is a common practice.

story.en: The story told is of King Mahidhvaja, a righteous king whose younger brother Vajradhvaja, jealous, took his life and buried him beneath a peepal tree. The king's spirit could not rest, and troubled travellers who passed that way. The sage Dhaumya, passing by, understood what had happened, kept the Apara Ekadashi and offered its merit to the king, and Mahidhvaja found peace. The story is told to show how far a single sincere observance, made for another, can reach.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu as Trivikrama with tulsi and a lamp, and hear the story of King Mahidhvaja.
Offer water or sherbet to people in the heat.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Jyeshtha Shukla Ekadashi, the strictest Ekadashi, kept without even water.

traditions.en: 'Nirjala' means without water. Those who keep it fully go from sunrise to the next sunrise without food or water, in the hottest weeks of the year. Because of the hardship, tradition places great value on giving water: people set up stalls with cold water and sherbet, and give earthen pots, fans and umbrellas. It is also called Bhimseni Ekadashi. Those who cannot fast without water, for reasons of health or age, keep a gentler fast, which tradition fully accepts.

story.en: Bhima, the strongest of the Pandavas, loved his food and could not keep the twenty-four Ekadashis that his mother and brothers kept. He went to the sage Vyasa and asked if there were any way. Vyasa told him to keep just one Ekadashi, Jyeshtha Shukla Ekadashi, without food or water from sunrise to sunrise, and it would hold the place of all the others. Bhima kept it, and the day has been called Bhimseni Ekadashi since. The story is a gentle one: it makes room for those who find the full discipline hard.

en: Decide honestly how you will keep it; if you have any health condition, are pregnant, elderly or on medication, keep a gentle fast with water instead.
Eat and drink well the evening before.
On Ekadashi, worship Vishnu in the morning with tulsi and a lamp.
Give water: fill pots, set up a water stall, or give earthen pots, fans or umbrellas.
Keep the day calm and indoors in the heat; chant or read.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi, starting with water and something light.

summary.en: Ashadha Krishna Ekadashi (Jyeshtha in the amanta reckoning).

traditions.en: Coming just before the monsoon, Yogini Ekadashi is kept with a fast, worship of Vishnu and the peepal tree, and giving to those in need. Tradition holds it in especially high regard, and many keep it as a day of prayer and quiet.

story.en: The story told is of Hemamali, a gardener in the service of Kubera, whose task was to bring fresh flowers each morning for Kubera's worship of Shiva. One morning, lingering with his wife, he did not come. Kubera, angered, sent him from Alaka, and Hemamali wandered the earth, unwell and unhappy. At last he reached the ashram of the sage Markandeya, who listened kindly and told him of Yogini Ekadashi. Hemamali kept it with a full heart, his health returned, and he went home to Alaka.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu with tulsi and a lamp, and offer water at a peepal tree if one is near.
Hear the story of Hemamali and give food or water to someone.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Shravana Krishna Ekadashi (Ashadha in the amanta reckoning), the first Ekadashi of chaturmas's dark fortnight.

traditions.en: Devotees fast, worship Vishnu, and especially honour the tulsi plant: watering it, lighting a lamp before it and offering its leaves. Many light a ghee lamp before Vishnu through the evening. It falls in the rains, a season of reflection.

story.en: The story told is of a hot-tempered landowner who, in a quarrel, struck a Brahmin, who fell and did not survive. Overwhelmed with remorse, the landowner wished to make amends, but the village would not let him take part in its rites. A sage told him to keep Kamika Ekadashi with sincerity, worshipping Vishnu with tulsi, and he did so. The story is told of how heartfelt remorse and a turn toward goodness are honoured in tradition, and how the village took him back.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Water the tulsi plant, light a lamp before it and offer tulsi leaves to Vishnu.
Keep a ghee lamp lit before Vishnu in the evening.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Shravana Shukla Ekadashi, traditionally kept by couples praying for children.

traditions.en: 'Putrada' means 'giver of children'. Couples hoping for a child often keep this fast together, and parents keep it for their children's wellbeing. Vishnu is worshipped as Bal Gopal, the child Krishna. In the South this Ekadashi is also called Pavitropana Ekadashi, when a pavitra, a woven thread, is offered to Vishnu.

story.en: King Mahijit of Mahishmati ruled his people well but had no children, and the sorrow weighed on him and his kingdom. His ministers went to the sage Lomasha, who saw that the king in an earlier life had once turned a thirsty cow away from water. He advised that the king and his people keep the Shravana Shukla Ekadashi together and offer its merit to the king. They did, and in time a son was born to the royal couple, and the kingdom celebrated.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans; couples may keep it together.
Worship Bal Gopal or Vishnu with tulsi, butter and a lamp; hear the story of King Mahijit.
Give water to animals and food to children in need.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Bhadrapada Krishna Ekadashi (Shravana in the amanta reckoning), also called Annada Ekadashi.

traditions.en: Coming a few days after Janmashtami, Aja Ekadashi is kept with a fast, worship of Vishnu and a night of bhajans in many homes. The story of King Harishchandra is read, and people reflect on keeping one's word through hard times.

story.en: Harishchandra, king of Ayodhya, was famed for never telling a lie. Tested by the sage Vishvamitra, he gave up his kingdom to keep a promise, and to pay the sage's fee he sold his wife and son and himself, ending as a keeper of the cremation ground at Kashi. Through every hardship he did not break his word. When his young son died and his wife came to the ground unable to pay the fee, Harishchandra, heartbroken, still asked for it as his duty required. The sage Gautama had told him of Aja Ekadashi, which he kept, and the story ends with the gods appearing, restoring his son and kingdom, and honouring his truthfulness.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu with tulsi and a lamp, and read the story of Harishchandra.
Sing bhajans in the evening, and reflect on a promise you mean to keep.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Bhadrapada Shukla Ekadashi: Vishnu turns onto his side in his sleep; also Vamana Ekadashi.

traditions.en: Also called Parivartini Ekadashi, from 'turning'. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu in his Vamana form, the dwarf brahmin, with curd rice and flowers. In Maharashtra it falls during Ganeshotsav, and it is a day of quiet worship in the middle of chaturmas.

story.en: The asura king Bali, grandson of Prahlad, was generous and powerful and had come to rule the three worlds. Vishnu came to his sacrifice as Vamana, a small brahmin boy, and asked for just three steps of land. Bali, against his teacher's warning, gladly agreed. Vamana grew to cosmic size: with one step he covered the earth, with the second the heavens, and for the third Bali offered his own head. Moved by his generosity, Vishnu gave him the underworld to rule and promised to stay as his guardian. On this Ekadashi, tradition says, Vishnu, sleeping through chaturmas, turns onto his side.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vamana or Vishnu with tulsi, flowers and curd, and hear the story of Bali.
Give something with an open hand, as Bali did.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Ashvin Krishna Ekadashi (Bhadrapada in the amanta reckoning), in Pitru Paksha, kept for ancestors.

traditions.en: Falling within Pitru Paksha, Indira Ekadashi joins the Ekadashi fast to the remembrance of ancestors. Families keep the fast, worship Vishnu as Shaligram, and many perform a shraddha for their forebears on this day, offering food to Brahmins, cows and crows.

story.en: King Indrasena of Mahishmati was visited by the sage Narada, who brought news of the king's late father: in the afterlife, he wished his son would remember him. Narada told Indrasena how to keep the Ekadashi of Ashvin's dark fortnight, with shraddha for his father on the day before and fasting and worship on Ekadashi, and to offer its merit to him. The king kept it with his family and his people, and Narada later told him that his father was at peace. The story is the reason this Ekadashi is kept in remembrance of one's elders.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu with tulsi and a lamp, and remember your ancestors by name.
If your family does, offer food to Brahmins, cows or crows, and give to those in need.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Ashvin Shukla Ekadashi, the day after Dussehra.

traditions.en: Coming right after Vijayadashami, Papankusha Ekadashi is kept with a fast and worship of Vishnu as Padmanabha, the lotus-naveled. Giving is especially valued: food, clothes, grain, an umbrella or footwear. The name speaks of an 'ankusha', the goad that steers an elephant, and the day is seen as a time to steer oneself back toward good conduct.

story.en: The story told is of Krodhana, a hunter in the Vindhya mountains who lived harshly and gave no thought to others. Near the end of his life, frightened and alone, he came to the ashram of the sage Angira and asked whether a life like his could still turn toward good. Angira told him of the Ekadashi of Ashvin's bright fortnight. Krodhana kept it with complete sincerity, and the story says that he found peace. The name 'Papankusha' is read as the goad that turns a person away from wrongdoing, at any point in life.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
Worship Vishnu as Padmanabha with lotuses or other flowers, tulsi and a lamp.
Give food, clothes or something useful to someone in need.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Kartika Krishna Ekadashi (Ashvin in the amanta reckoning), four days before Diwali.

traditions.en: Named after Rama, a name of Lakshmi, this Ekadashi is kept with a fast and worship of Vishnu and Lakshmi together, as homes are being cleaned and readied for Diwali. Many light lamps before tulsi in the evening, as is done throughout Kartika.

story.en: King Muchukunda, a devotee of Vishnu, had his whole kingdom keep Ekadashi. His daughter Chandrabhaga married Prince Shobhana, who was frail and found fasting very hard. When Rama Ekadashi came while Shobhana was visiting, Chandrabhaga, torn, encouraged him to keep it with everyone, and Shobhana, too weak, passed away in the night. Through the merit of the fast, the story says, he was given a beautiful city on Mount Mandarachala, but it could not last without a devotee's support. Chandrabhaga, who had kept every Ekadashi since childhood, journeyed there, offered him the merit of her own fasts, and the two lived together in the city, steadied by her devotion.

en: Eat a light, grain-free meal the evening before.
Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans; if fasting is hard for you, keep a gentle fast, as the story itself suggests.
Worship Vishnu and Lakshmi together with tulsi, flowers and a lamp.
Light a lamp before the tulsi plant in the evening.
Break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Kartika Shukla Ekadashi: Vishnu wakes from his four-month sleep; chaturmas ends.

traditions.en: Also called Prabodhini Ekadashi and Dev Uthani Ekadashi, it ends chaturmas. In the evening, families draw Vishnu's footprints and a sugarcane canopy in the courtyard, place seasonal produce, water chestnuts, sugarcane, sweet potato and jujube, under it, and wake the god with bells, conch and songs: 'Utho Dev, baitho Dev'. Disciplines kept since Devshayani Ekadashi end today. Tulsi Vivah follows, and the season for weddings begins. In Pandharpur, the Kartiki Wari reaches Vitthal.

story.en: Having entered yoga nidra on Devshayani Ekadashi, Vishnu wakes on this day after four months. One telling explains the sleep itself: after a long struggle against the asura Shankhasura, Vishnu rested in the ocean of milk, and the gods agreed to keep watch through the rains. Another tells that Vishnu promised Bali, ruler of the underworld, that he would dwell with him for four months of every year; on Devutthana Ekadashi he returns. Either way, the household wakes him with joy, and the year's celebrations can begin again.

en: Fast on Ekadashi from grains and beans.
In the evening, draw Vishnu's footprints in the courtyard with rice flour or chalk and set up a small sugarcane canopy.
Place seasonal fruit and vegetables under it, light lamps around it, and worship Vishnu.
Wake him with a bell or conch and the song 'Utho Dev, baitho Dev'.
End any chaturmas discipline today, and break the fast the next morning during Dvadashi.

summary.en: Margashirsha Krishna Ekadashi (Kartika in the amanta reckoning): the birth of Ekadashi herself.

traditions.en: 'Utpanna' means 'arisen'. This is traditionally the Ekadashi on which people who wish to begin keeping Ekadashis start, since it remembers the day Ekadashi was born. Devotees fast and worship Vishnu, and hear the story of Ekadashi Devi.

story.en: The asura Mura had driven the gods from heaven, and Vishnu fought him for a thousand years. Tired, Vishnu went to rest in a cave at Badrikashram. Mura followed him there, meaning to strike while he slept. From Vishnu's body arose a radiant goddess, who faced Mura and overcame him. When Vishnu woke and saw what had happened, he named her Ekadashi, since she had appeared on the eleventh day, and granted that those who keep her day would be dear to him. From that day, the story says, Ekadashi has been kept.
